# Master Complexity Table — Deep Analysis Report

**Corpus:** 6,117 unique real-user questions (4 elicitation stages, 8 personas, 96 participants)
**Classifier:** GPT-5.5, frozen two-axis rubric (`scripts/J_complexity_master_table.py`)
**Analysis:** `scripts/K_master_table_analysis.py` — fully reproducible; every number below is regenerated by re-running it
**Data quality:** 8 structural invariants checked → **0 violations in 6,117 rows** (`00_data_quality_report.md`)
**Date:** 2026-06-25

---

## How to Read This Report

This report analyses a corpus of **6,117 natural language questions** collected from real building users via Amazon MTurk. Participants were asked to imagine they could talk to their smart building and write down questions they would want answered. Questions were collected across four structured stages — open-ended, sensor-prompted, scenario-based, and goal-oriented — from 96 participants representing 8 personas (students, occupants, guests, health-and-safety officers, sustainability/energy teams, building owners, IT staff, and facility managers).

Every question was then independently graded by an LLM (GPT-5.5) on **two separate difficulty axes**: how hard the question is for a *human* to reason about, and how hard it is for an *automated system* to answer properly. The gap between these two scores is the central finding.

**Who this is for:** colleagues, reviewers, and anyone else who wants to understand what the corpus analysis found and what the numbers mean — without needing to run the code themselves.

---

## Section 0 — Key Concepts and Terminology

Read this section before the results. Every term used later in the report is defined here.

---

### 0.1 The Two Axes: Surface vs. Latent Complexity

Every question in the corpus is rated on a **1–6 scale on two completely independent axes**.

---

#### Axis 1: Surface Level (Cognitive Complexity)

> **What it measures:** How hard is this question for a *human* to think about?

This captures the type of human reasoning the question requires — recall, comparison, inference, causal thinking, or open-ended strategic reasoning. It does **not** depend on whether a computer can answer it; it is purely about the mental effort a person would expend.

| Level | Name | What it means | Example question |
|---|---|---|---|
| **L1** | Factual Recall | Recall a single fact; trivial cognitive load; clear answer | *"What floor is the cafe on?"* |
| **L2** | Comparative Analysis | Compare two or more things; slightly more cognitive effort | *"Is Floor 3 warmer than Floor 5 right now?"* |
| **L3** | Inferential Reasoning | Draw a conclusion from available information; moderate reasoning | *"Based on the CO2 levels, is this room well-ventilated?"* |
| **L4** | Causal Diagnosis | Identify cause-and-effect relationships; high reasoning load | *"Why has energy use risen even though occupancy dropped?"* |
| **L5** | Systemic Synthesis | Reason across multiple interacting systems; synthesise into a unified picture; high uncertainty | *"How do HVAC, occupancy, and window state interact to affect IAQ on Floor 4?"* |
| **L6** | Meta / Strategic Reasoning | Open-ended, goal-level, or ethical reasoning; highly ambiguous; no single right answer | *"How do I make this building more environmentally friendly?"* |

**Key property:** Surface level is rated on the phrasing and reasoning type of the question, not its data requirements. A simple yes/no question asked in one sentence is usually L1 or L2 regardless of how hard it is to answer technically.

---

#### Axis 2: Latent Level (Architectural Complexity)

> **What it measures:** How hard is it for an *automated smart-building system* to answer this question as well as a knowledgeable human expert would?

This captures what the system would need to do — look up a fact, run a statistical analysis, fuse data from multiple sources, orchestrate a multi-step plan, or control physical equipment. It depends entirely on system effort, not on the difficulty of the question phrasing.

| Level | Name | What the system needs to do | Example question and why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **L1** | Factual Recall | Single ontology or metadata lookup; no analytics | *"What type of sensor is in Room 402?"* — one SPARQL query |
| **L2** | Comparative Analysis | A few reads + light aggregation or comparison | *"Which floor has the highest CO2 right now?"* — query all floors, rank |
| **L3** | Inferential Reasoning | Multi-hop retrieval or derived values across linked datasets | *"Which zones have both high CO2 and high temperature?"* — join two sensor streams |
| **L4** | Causal Diagnosis | Time-series retrieval + statistical analytics (correlation, anomaly detection, causal inference) | *"Is this room always stuffy on Monday mornings?"* — time-series pull, trend analysis |
| **L5** | Systemic Synthesis | Multi-system data fusion + modelling/forecasting + multi-section report with visuals | *"Predict next week's energy use and identify anomalies likely to occur"* — forecast + model + visualise |
| **L6** | Meta / Strategic Reasoning | Cross-domain orchestration, planning, actuation/control loop, or a novel method not yet built | *"If water flow is detected for 2 hours at night, automatically close the valve"* — ECA rule engine + BMS write-back + sensor not yet present |

**Critical property:** Latent level is **independent** of surface level. A question can be L1 surface (sounds trivially simple to a human) yet L6 latent (requires machinery that doesn't exist yet). This independence is the entire reason for having two axes — and the source of the main finding.

---

### 0.2 The Iceberg Effect

> **Definition:** A question exhibits the iceberg effect when its latent (architectural) complexity is significantly higher than its surface (cognitive) complexity — i.e., it looks easy but is hard to answer properly.

The name comes from an iceberg: only a small fraction is visible above the water (what the question *looks like*), while the vast majority is hidden below the surface (what it *costs* the system to answer truthfully).

**Measurement in this study:**

- **Any iceberg:** latent level > surface level (63.3% of all questions)
- **Moderate iceberg:** latent level ≥ surface level + 2 (35.2%)
- **Extreme iceberg:** surface ≤ 2 AND latent ≥ surface + 3 (770 questions, 12.6%)

**Concrete example of an extreme iceberg:**

> *"Can the lifts 'learn' that the cafeteria floor is the priority destination at exactly 12:05 PM?"*

- **Surface level: L1** — It is phrased as a yes/no capability check. A human answers it in one second.
- **Latent level: L6** — A truthful system answer requires: occupancy detection (sensor not present), time-series learning algorithm, BMS lift controller write-back, a closed-loop control loop, and an approval workflow. None of these exist yet.

The iceberg effect means that **question phrasing is a misleading signal for system design**. You cannot estimate how hard it is to build a conversational building interface by reading the questions — you must look at what the system needs to do to answer them correctly.

---

### 0.3 Answerability Categories

Each question is assigned one of three answerability labels based on whether the current OntoSage system (deployed on Building 1, Abacws, Cardiff University) can answer it today:

| Category | Meaning | Count | % |
|---|---|---|---|
| **full** | The system can answer this completely today, without any new components or data | 1,385 | 22.6% |
| **partial** | The system can give a useful but incomplete answer (e.g., data exists for Floor 5 only, not all floors) | 207 | 3.4% |
| **requires_extension** | The system cannot answer this truthfully without a new data source, sensor, integration, or software component | 4,525 | 74.0% |

`requires_extension` does **not** mean "impossible" or "out of scope". It means the right answer exists but requires adding something that is not yet present in the deployed system. Every `requires_extension` question has a `[NEW]` marker in its capability-gap field naming exactly what is missing.

---

### 0.4 Answer Basis

Each question is also tagged with how the answer is sourced:

| Basis | Meaning | Count |
|---|---|---|
| **building-data** | Needs this building's specific sensor readings, topology, or metadata | 4,001 |
| **hybrid** | Applies a general norm (e.g., a comfort standard) to this building's live data | 1,345 |
| **general-knowledge** | Answerable from general world knowledge with no building data at all (e.g., "how does CO2 affect concentration?") — the LLM answers directly | 771 |

`general-knowledge` questions automatically receive `latent_level = 1` and `answerability = full` because the system can answer them with a single LLM call — no pipelines or sensors needed.

---

### 0.5 The `[NEW]` Marker and Capability Gaps

Every question tagged `requires_extension` contains one or more `[NEW] <item>` tags in its classification record. These tags name the specific missing component — for example:

- `[NEW] occupancy sensor feed`
- `[NEW] energy metering integration`
- `[NEW] BMS write-back actuation`

Aggregating all `[NEW]` items across 6,117 rows produces the **capability-gap taxonomy** in Section 4 and file `T5_new_capability_gaps.csv`. This taxonomy is the engineering backlog derived directly from what users actually ask.

---

### 0.6 Elicitation Stages

Questions were collected in four distinct stages to ensure diversity:

| Stage | Method | Count | What it surfaces |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stage 1** | Open-ended: "What would you ask your building?" | 1,636 | Unprompted, intuitive questions |
| **Stage 2** | Sensor-prompted: shown a list of sensor types | 1,723 | Data-aware questions about specific streams |
| **Stage 3** | Scenario-based: given a situation (e.g., "it's a hot afternoon") | 1,449 | Contextual, diagnostic questions |
| **Stage 4** | Goal-oriented: given a goal (e.g., "reduce energy use") | 1,309 | Strategic, high-level intent questions |

Stages 3 and 4 produce harder questions (higher surface and latent levels on average) because the scenarios and goals naturally invite causal and systemic thinking.

---

### 0.7 Persona Groups

Participants are grouped into 8 personas for analysis:

| Persona | Who they are | Typical question style |
|---|---|---|
| Students / Researchers | University students and academic researchers | Conceptual, exploratory, high-latent |
| Occupants / Tenants | Day-to-day building users | Comfort-focused, conversational, deceptively complex |
| Guests / Visitors | One-time or infrequent visitors | Wayfinding, simple factual, occasionally strategic |
| Health & Safety Officers | Compliance and safety roles | Regulatory, procedural, predictive (evacuation/compliance) |
| Sustainability / Energy teams | Energy and net-zero specialists | Energy-saturated, deepest analytical/predictive appetite |
| Building Owners | Decision-makers with strategic oversight | High-level, policy, general-knowledge-heavy |
| IT / Data Scientists | Technical staff managing systems | Diagnostic, system-level, explicit |
| Facility Managers | Staff responsible for building operations | Operational, data-heavy, explicit |

## 1. Executive Summary

Every question was graded on two independent 1–6 axes:

- **Surface (cognitive) level** — how hard the question is for a *human* to reason about.
- **Latent (architectural) level** — how hard it is for an *automated system* to answer it as well as a knowledgeable human would.

| Headline | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean surface level | **2.40** (most questions read as simple recall or inference) |
| Mean latent level | **3.37** (most questions require at least multi-hop analytics to answer) |
| Questions architecturally harder than they look (latent > surface) | **63.3%** |
| Extreme "iceberg" questions (surface ≤ 2, latent ≥ 3 levels higher) | **770 (12.6%)** |
| Fully answerable by the current bldg1 deployment | **22.6%** |
| Need a data/capability extension (not new reasoning) | **74.0%** |
| Latent-L6 questions (closed-loop autonomy / cross-domain orchestration) | **645 (10.5%)** |
| Surface-L6 questions (meta/strategic/ethical) | **129 (2.1%)** |

**The single most important result:** the difficulty of human-building conversation is dominated by the *latent* axis, not the cognitive one. People phrase architecturally enormous requests as trivial yes/no questions. The gap between how questions *look* and what they *cost to answer* is the central design problem — and it is invisible to any analysis that only looks at question phrasing.

---

## 2. The Complexity Iceberg (key figure: `F2_level_vs_latent_heatmap.png`)

The latent distribution is shifted a full level to the right of the surface/cognitive one (`F1_level_distributions.png`). The table below shows how many questions fall at each level on each axis:

| Level | Level Name | Surface (cognitive) count | Latent (architectural) count |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1 | Factual Recall | 2,378 | 1,049 |
| L2 | Comparative Analysis | 790 | 706 |
| L3 | Inferential Reasoning | 1,971 | 1,490 |
| L4 | Causal Diagnosis | 208 | 1,309 |
| L5 | Systemic Synthesis | 641 | 918 |
| L6 | Meta / Strategic Reasoning | 129 | 645 |

**How to read this table:** Only 208 questions *read* as requiring causal diagnosis (surface L4), but **1,309 require** time-series analytics to answer properly (latent L4). The question *"is my office always this stuffy?"* is surface L1 — it sounds like a one-word yes/no. But the truthful answer needs historical CO2 time-series, a trend analysis, a comparison to comfort thresholds, and a causal inference about HVAC scheduling. That is latent L4.

Similarly: only 129 questions read as meta-strategic (surface L6), but 645 require cross-domain orchestration to answer (latent L6). The phrasing dramatically underestimates system complexity.

**770 extreme icebergs** (`T2_iceberg_questions.csv`) look like simple capability checks but demand latent L5–L6 machinery. Representative examples:

> *"If water flow is detected for 2 hours straight in a bathroom at night, can the system automatically shut off that valve?"* — surface L1, latent L6
> *"Can the lifts 'learn' that the cafeteria floor is the priority destination at exactly 12:05 PM?"* — surface L1, latent L6
> *"Can the system predict a Peak Demand event from the afternoon weather forecast and start pre-cooling?"* — surface L1, latent L6
> *"Could escalators switch to standby when corridors are empty?"* — surface L1, latent L6

A human answers these "yes/no" in one second. A truthful *system* answer requires an event-condition-action rule engine, sensor feeds that do not exist yet, predictive models, and an actuation loop.

---

## 3. The Hardest Questions, in Four Archetypes — and How We Solve Each

The top-60 composite-difficulty ranking is in `T1_top60_hardest_questions.csv`; the hardest question per persona in `T7_hardest_per_persona.csv`. They cluster into four archetypes:

### Archetype A — Autonomy Mandates (the genuinely hardest class)

> *"Can you make the building more eco-friendly?"* (Occupant — surface L6 / latent L6)
> *"Could we develop a way for our building to automatically shift large HVAC loads to off-peak times when more renewable energy is available?"* (Occupant — L5/L6)
> *"can you self manage yourself"* (Building Owner — L5/L6)
> *"How do I make you more environmentally-friendly?"* (Student — L6/L6)

These are not queries at all — they are **delegated open-ended goals**. The user hands the system an objective ("be greener", "optimise", "self-manage") and expects it to decompose the goal, plan, act, and report. No retrieval pipeline answers these.

**Solution path:** goal-decomposition planning on top of the existing LangGraph multi-step planner. The planner node already decomposes compound queries; the extension is (1) a *goal → measurable sub-objectives* decomposition step (e.g. "eco-friendly" → energy/peak/waste/comfort KPIs), (2) per-objective routing into existing pipelines (analytics, forecast, recommend), and (3) an honest capability report: *here is what I can measure today, here is what acting on it would require*. Crucially OntoSage **already routes actuation to a `control` intent that declines safely** — the right behaviour until BMS write-back is wired with RBAC guardrails. Full autonomy is the *last* phase of the roadmap (§6), not the first.

### Archetype B — Closed-Loop Automation Icebergs (largest hard class: 645 latent-L6 rows, `T4_latent6_orchestration.csv`)

The "can the building automatically X when Y" pattern above. Today, OntoSage's capability KB (Qdrant) can honestly answer *whether* the building can do it. Making the building actually do it requires:

1. **An event-condition-action (ECA) rule layer** — a generic rules service (trigger: sensor condition; action: notify or actuate) configured per building in YAML, not code. ~80% of the 645 questions instantiate the same ECA template with different sensors/actions.
2. **BMS write-back** (1,009 question-mentions) behind RBAC `control:write` permission and an approval workflow.
3. The missing trigger feeds themselves (occupancy, water, energy — see §4).

This is the strongest engineering argument in the corpus: *one* generic rule engine + *one* actuation gateway covers hundreds of distinct user wishes.

### Archetype C — Causal/Diagnostic Questions Blocked by Missing Data

> *"Why has energy use risen despite lower occupancy?"*-type questions: surface L4, latent L5.

The reasoning machinery (analytics sandbox, anomaly detection, forecasting, correlation) **already exists** in OntoSage. These questions fail only because bldg1 has no energy meters, occupancy sensors, or weather feed. They need **zero new reasoning code** — only data onboarding (§4). This is why "74.0% requires extension" is much less alarming than it sounds.

### Archetype D — Meta/Ethical/Social Questions (129 rows, `T3_level6_meta_questions.csv`)

> *"Would you be looking for people having an argument? Looking for signs of abuse? How would you step in?"* (Occupant)
> *"Who is the judge of the results? How do you feel about this?"* (Occupant)
> *"How does the building plan upgrades to meet future sustainability standards?"* (Student)

Users probe the system's **agency, judgement, and ethics** — surveillance boundaries, accountability, self-improvement. These are answered not with data but with **policy**: a per-building governance document (what the system monitors, what it will never infer, who reviews decisions) served through the capability KB. This is a deployment artifact (a YAML/markdown file in `input/<bldg>/`), not code — and it is a publishable finding that real users ask these unprompted.

**Honest caveat:** a number of top-ranked rows are elliptical fragments ("can you optimize", "maintenance?", "emissions mimi"). The rubric correctly scores them highly ambiguous → L6. The system answer is the existing `clarification` intent; the analysis answer is that ~2% of real queries are too underspecified to classify meaningfully, which itself motivates the clarification pipeline.

---

## 4. What Exactly Is Missing — the Capability-Gap Taxonomy (`T5`, `F4_new_gaps.png`)

Every `[NEW]` item across 6,117 rows, canonicalised into a stable taxonomy. These are the things users need that the current system cannot provide:

| Gap | Questions needing it | Type of fix |
|---|---|---|
| Occupancy sensing (incl. PIR/motion/door) | 1,325 (21.7%) | new sensor feed |
| BMS actuation / write-back (incl. setpoints) | 1,009 (16.5%) | integration + safety guardrails |
| Energy metering | 933 (15.3%) | new sensor feed |
| Live streams, floors 0–4 | 855 (14.0%) | connect already-modelled sensors |
| Calendar / room-booking API | 517 (8.5%) | external API (config) |
| Weather feed | 502 (8.2%) | external API (config) — free, keyless |
| Lighting sensing/control | 424 (6.9%) | new feed |
| Access / security systems | 415 (6.8%) | integration |
| Policy / document KB | 333 (5.4%) | **drop documents in `input/` — no code** |
| Maintenance / CMMS records | 323 (5.3%) | integration |
| Extended IAQ (PM/VOC/NO₂) | 323 (5.3%) | new sensors |
| Ontology metadata enrichment (capacity, tenants, quiet zones…) | 304 (5.0%) | **edit TTL/YAML — no code** |
| Noise / acoustic | 285 (4.7%) | new sensors |
| Water metering | 231 (3.8%) | new feed |
| Carbon / ESG data | 151 (2.5%) | new feed / integration |

Two structural findings:

1. **Concentration:** the top-8 gaps alone fully unblock **48.8%** of all `requires_extension` questions. A handful of feeds, not hundreds of features, is the real backlog.
2. **The long tail is irreducible:** beyond the named categories sit ~5,000 mentions of niche needs whose *most frequent* item appears only 4 times (fire-alarm feed, gas meter, fridge temperature, Wi-Fi controller API, vending-machine inventory…). **No amount of feature-building covers this tail.** The only scalable answer is the architecture OntoSage already follows — generic, config-driven onboarding (TTL + YAML + adapters) so each niche need is a *data drop*, not a development task. The tail is the empirical justification for the input-folder design.

Note also rows tagged "Ontology metadata enrichment" and "Policy / document KB" (637 questions combined): these need **no new sensors and no new code** — only richer input files. They are the cheapest 10% win available.

## 5. Who Asks the Hard Questions? (counterintuitive — `F5_persona_difficulty.png`, `T6`)

| Persona | n | mean surface level | mean latent level | % requires extension | % general-knowledge |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sustainability / Energy | 375 | 3.08 | **4.20** | 88.3 | 4.0 |
| Students / Researchers | 1,335 | 2.41 | **3.61** | 81.9 | 5.0 |
| Occupants / Tenants | 1,194 | 2.14 | **3.48** | 79.2 | 4.4 |
| Health & Safety Officers | 329 | 2.91 | 3.47 | 71.4 | 14.6 |
| Guests / Visitors | 1,378 | 2.14 | 3.28 | 75.2 | 9.6 |
| Facility Managers | 410 | 2.69 | 3.03 | 63.7 | 23.7 |
| Building Owners | 421 | 2.42 | 2.94 | 60.6 | 29.7 |
| IT / Data Scientists | 675 | 2.54 | **2.87** | 54.4 | 34.8 |

**How to read this table:** "mean surface level" is how hard the *phrasing* of their questions is; "mean latent level" is how hard it would be to answer them properly. "% requires extension" is the share that cannot be answered by the current system at all. "% general-knowledge" is the share that need no building data — the LLM answers from general world knowledge.

**The counterintuitive result holds, with a twist.** Two groups demand the most architecture. The first is exactly the people with the *least* technical knowledge — students, occupants and guests phrase high-latent automation wishes ("can the building just do X for me"). The second is the *Sustainability / Energy* specialists, who now top the latent scale (4.20) and the requires-extension share (88.3%): their net-zero, forecasting and optimisation questions land squarely on the data feeds bldg1 does not yet have (energy metering, occupancy, weather, carbon). By contrast the IT, Building-Owner and Facility-Manager professionals ask questions they could partly answer themselves — conceptual, general-knowledge, lower system effort. Either way the system, not the user, must absorb the complexity — direct evidence for the **zero-knowledge-interaction design goal**.

The naive assumption — that *general* technical expertise predicts system stress — does not hold: the heaviest demand comes from lay delegators and from domain specialists whose domain is the least instrumented, not from technically literate professionals in general. The design conclusion is the same: the system must absorb complexity because the people who stress it most are the least equipped (or least inclined) to do that work themselves.

---

## 6. Implementation Roadmap (mapped to the existing OntoSage architecture)

OntoSage today: LangGraph orchestrator (26 auto-registered intents), GraphDB Brick/BACnet/ASHRAE-223 ontology, MySQL time-series, sandboxed analytics, ARIMA/ETS forecasting, agentic RAG, Qdrant capability KB, floor-plan/spatial pipeline, report intake, multi-step planner, conversation memory. New intents are added via YAML + one node method — no graph edits. Buildings are swapped by dropping files in `input/<id>/`.

The roadmap orders work by **questions unblocked per unit of engineering**, preserving the no-hardcoding principle (every phase ends in *config*, not building-specific code):

| Phase | Work | Questions unblocked | Effort | New code? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Input enrichment** | Richer TTL metadata (room capacity, tenant map, quiet zones) + policy/governance docs into capability KB | ~637 (10%) | days | **none** — files only |
| **2. Connect floors 0–4** | Wire already-modelled sensors to live MySQL streams | 855 | days–weeks | none (UUIDs already modelled) |
| **3. Generic external-feed adapter** | One config-driven adapter class (`type: rest/mqtt`, auth, field-map, Brick class) registered per building in YAML; first instances: weather (free/keyless), calendar, tariffs | ~900 + entire long tail becomes config | 2–3 weeks | **once, generically** |
| **4. Sensor expansion** | Occupancy, energy, IAQ, noise, water feeds via Phase-3 adapter + TTL entries | ~2,500 question-mentions | hardware + config | none beyond Phase 3 |
| **5. ECA rule engine** | Generic event-condition-action service, rules in per-building YAML; actions = notify first, actuate later | most of 645 latent-L6 | 3–4 weeks | once, generically |
| **6. BMS write-back + guardrails** | Actuation gateway behind RBAC `control:write`, approval workflow, audit log | 1,009 question-mentions | longest; safety-critical | once |
| **7. Goal-decomposition planner** | "Make it eco-friendly" → KPI sub-goals → existing pipelines → honest capability report | Archetype A (§3) | research-grade | extends existing planner |

In parallel, the corpus directly supports the **concept-layer ontology extending Brick** (the human-vocabulary → Brick-class → analytic-recipe mapping, e.g. "stuffy" → `brick:CO2_Level_Sensor` + threshold recipe). The 6,117 questions are the mining corpus for that vocabulary; because Brick classes are building-independent, the layer is authored once and inherited by every Brick-conformant building. That is the novel, publishable contribution; Phases 1–6 are the engineering substrate it runs on.

---

## 7. Anticipated Supervisor Questions — Direct Answers

**"What is the toughest question users asked?"**
By composite score: *"Can you make the building more eco-friendly?"* (surface L6 / latent L6) — a four-word open-ended autonomy mandate requiring goal decomposition, multi-domain data fusion, optimisation, actuation, and ethics, none of which the user is aware of. The runner-up class is the closed-loop iceberg, best exemplified by the night-time water-valve question (surface L1 / latent L6).

**"What made you think deeper?"**
Three things. (1) The iceberg effect: 63.3% of questions are architecturally harder than they read, so question phrasing is a *misleading* signal for system design. (2) The inversion: lay users and energy specialists demand more architecture than general-purpose technical experts. (3) The irreducible long tail: the most frequent unmet niche need appears only 4 times in 6,117 questions — feature-building can never win; only generic data-driven onboarding scales.

**"How will you solve it?"**
Not per-question — per-*mechanism*. 74.0% of questions are blocked by ~8 concentrated data gaps plus one long tail; the fix is (a) two zero-code phases (input enrichment, floor connection), (b) one generic feed adapter that turns every future integration into YAML, (c) one generic ECA rule engine for the automation class, (d) guarded actuation, and (e) the concept-layer ontology so any Brick building inherits the conversational vocabulary. After phases 1–4 the fully-answerable share rises from 22.6% to an estimated ~70%+ without any building-specific code.

**"How do you know the LLM classifications are trustworthy?"**
Three layers: (1) frozen rubric with worked calibration examples injected into every call (no drift); (2) eight structural invariants validated post-hoc — **0 violations in 6,117 rows**; (3) the planned inter-rater check: re-classify a ~150-row sample with a second model (Anthropic Claude via the same script, `--provider anthropic`) and report Cohen's κ. Step (2) is done; step (3) is one command away.

**"Why two axes instead of one difficulty score?"**
Because they disagree on 63.3% of the corpus, and the disagreement *is* the finding. A single score would average away the iceberg effect — the exact phenomenon a conversational building interface must engineer around.

**"What does 'requires extension' actually mean — is most of the corpus unanswerable?"**
No. It means the current deployment is missing a specific data source or component. 74.0% of questions say "I need occupancy data" or "I need an ECA rule engine" — not "this is impossible". The reasoning machinery (analytics, forecasting, correlation) is already built. It is a *data* and *integration* backlog, not an AI research problem.
